blocks.text: intro
A dry, distant tick starts alone. Four bars of uneven banjo gather around it; low tuba enters slightly late. Room noise and a chair creak before the voice.
verse 1
One close, weathered male lead throughout; affectionate but uneasy, then sly. Banjo and tuba leave holes while the tick keeps going. Each line comes a little sooner; clip 'do it again.'

My folks were kids in '62
They learned to duck; they taught me too
Keep your head down, count to ten
Wait for the all-clear, then do it again
Accordion offers one almost cheerful answer, then slips sour as the narrator admits the trick. Bowed bass holds under the last two lines; the tick moves closer.

They meant to keep me safe, I know
But fear's a thing that learns to grow
I learned to make a warning stick
Half a truth and half a trick
chorus

Instrumental band locks to the tick: low tuba ostinato, clipped banjo and accordion, heavy suitcase kick, scraped washboard. The rhythm subdivides; the same solo voice leans slightly ahead of the beat, with no other singers. One brief clarinet flourish flickers. Cut the band before the title, but leave the tick exposed.

We had a plan for staying in
No plan for coming out again
We sold the fear as revivalism
Called it the new survivalism
Two-bar instrumental turn: clarinet and accordion trade one fleeting bright phrase over the continuing tick; a dull metal scrape cuts it short.
verse 2
Hard drop to muted banjo and the now-audible tick; tuba rests. Keep the delivery plain and specific; the sheltering came from care.

COVID came; we stayed at home
Called our folks and wiped the phone
We made some soup, we learned the charts
We did our best to do our part
Rim taps double the tick; wavering accordion enters. The singer pushes through the last two lines in one breath, as though checking again before sleep.

Then every day became a year
We let the screen explain our fear
I lost a friend in a comment thread
Hit refresh instead of going to bed
chorus

Minor-key pulse returns denser: tuba repeats one figure, washboard fills the gaps, accordion chords tighten. A high clarinet glint vanishes. The lone lead sings more urgently, without harmonies or doubles. Cut the band before the title; the tick keeps moving underneath.

We had a plan for staying in
No plan for coming out again
We sold the fear as revivalism
Called it the new survivalism
verse 3
Abrupt cut to dry, close voice and the bare tick. An occasional low tuba note answers, but the count never breaks. Leave the first four lines exposed.

I was paid to bring the eyeballs in
I learned which fears would pull them in
Truth and lies? I let them blur
If the numbers rose, I called it work

Before 'I made the click,' everything but the tick falls away. Deliver 'I made the click, I took the pay' fast and bare; let the next lines tumble forward. Mechanical taps double the tick without covering the confession.

I made the click, I took the pay
Sat with the emptiness as it went away
Now the machine does it faster than me
And I taught it what makes people read
bridge
Kick lands in half-time against the unbroken tick. Washboard doubles over the last two lines; banjo climbs against a held, dissonant accordion chord. The subdivisions press forward.

We learned to duck, we learned to wait
We never practiced opening the gate
So here I am, a little late
With my hand on it anyway
final chorus

Full instrumental band returns with accumulated momentum, not triumph: low tuba, clipped accordion, banjo, kick, scraped washboard and metal orbit the tick. The same undoubled solo voice stays alone, slightly ahead of the pulse. Cut the band after 'out again' while the tick continues; one brighter chord touches 'Let somebody in,' then leaves the harmony unresolved.

We had a plan for staying in
We're learning how to come out again
Leave the door unlatched, let somebody in
Let somebody in
outro
Band cuts off mid-ring. Lone banjo and quiet radio murmur return; the tick is slower and farther away, but still audible.

There's still a can of soup downstairs
I keep it there; I like it there
The radio says the sky might fall
I turn it down and make a call
Almost spoken, tentative and close to the microphone. Let the tick stop on the word 'time.'
You got a little time?
Let the line hang without the tick. One soft tuba answer from across the room, then room tone.

notebook.style: Minor-key junkyard cabaret, mid-slow but always moving: a distant tick starts alone and persists through every drop, gathering subdivisions until the final word 'time.' One close, weathered male lead throughout, undoubled; no backing vocals, harmonies, choir, gang vocals or sung call-and-response, even in choruses. Uneven banjo, low tuba ostinato, clipped accordion, scraped washboard, suitcase kick, clarinet and metal. Build urgency through shorter breaths and denser rhythm, not a cheerful tempo jump. Verse 1 tightens toward 'do it again'; verse 2 presses through the screen and refresh; verse 3 strips to voice and tick, with 'I made the click' delivered fast and bare. Brief bright clarinet and accordion flashes vanish quickly. Bridge piles up subdivisions and dissonance; final chorus returns with accumulated force, still minor and unresolved. One brighter chord touches 'Let somebody in.' At the phone call, the tick stops on 'time'; tuba, room tone. No jaunty swing or triumphant swell.
